title: Diagonal Traversal of a Binary Tree
statement:
You are given a binary tree. Give every node a **diagonal index**: the root has index `0`, a right child has the **same** index as its parent, and a left child has index **parent + 1**. All nodes with the same index lie on one diagonal line running from the upper left to the lower right.

Output the node values grouped by diagonal, starting from diagonal `0`. Inside a diagonal, list the nodes by depth (shallower nodes first); nodes of the same depth are listed from left to right, exactly as a level-order traversal would visit them.

The tree has at least one node. Its height (number of nodes on the longest root-to-leaf path) is at most `5000`, so a recursive solution is safe in every supported language.

**Follow-up:** the original interview included several follow-ups on this problem that were not published. Be ready for variations such as printing only the last node of each diagonal, the sum of each diagonal, or doing the traversal both with a queue and with a recursive helper that carries the diagonal index.
inputFormat: A single line with the tree in level order, values separated by spaces, with `null` for a missing child (the children of a `null` are not listed, and trailing `null` values may be omitted). Values are integers.
outputFormat: Print one line per diagonal, starting with diagonal `0`. Each line contains the values of that diagonal separated by single spaces.

examples.explanation: Node 1 is the root (diagonal 0). Its right child 3 stays on diagonal 0 and so does 3's right child 6. Node 2 is a left child, so it starts diagonal 1, and its right child 5 stays on it. Node 4 is the left child of 2, so it forms diagonal 2.

Diagonal 0 holds only 10 (it has no right child). Diagonal 1 holds 5 and its right child 8. Diagonal 2 holds 3 (left child of 5), then 4 (right child of 3) and 7 (left child of 8). Both 4 and 7 are at depth 3, and 4 is to the left of 7.

hints: Which nodes share a diagonal? Moving to a right child never leaves the diagonal; moving to a left child moves to the next one.
Run a level-order traversal and store the diagonal index next to each node in the queue. Level order already gives the required order inside a diagonal.
Keep a list of lists indexed by diagonal and append each visited value to the list of its diagonal.
